As of 231 AM EDT Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A cold front is crossing New York and Vermont from north 
to south early this morning, producing widespread showers and 
drizzle as the parent low pressure ejects off eastern Canada into 
the northern Atlantic Ocean. The boundary is expected to stall out 
across the northeastern U.S. today and tonight as another fast 
moving clipper style system approaches from the west. This wave will 
increase southerly flow across the boundary as well as trigger 
moisture advection and increasing isentropic lift. This will result 
in an extended period of wet conditions for the forecast area. 
Southerly flow will be on the increase today, resulting in 
widespread rainfall amounts 1.00-1.50 inches, with lowest amounts 
occurring in southern Vermont and highest amounts likely on summits.
A few thunderstorms will be possible, especially this afternoon as 
the low pressure approaches and moves overhead this evening. This 
setup may promote some cold air damming east of the Greens, with 
highs today below 50 degrees in eastern Vermont. Elsewhere, we 
should have typical mid October highs reaching the 50s and lower 
60s. Rain chances will be on the decrease tonight as the low 
pressure moves away, but enough moisture lingers to keep lows on the 
milder side in the 40s to mid 50s.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A cold front is crossing New York and Vermont from north 
to south early this morning, then it is expected to stall out across 
the northeastern U.S. today and tonight. A low level jet that will 
amplify moisture across this stationary boundary will move through 
today, increasing southerly flow for the northern Champlain Valley. 
Mixing over the lake may be sufficient to intermittently bring some 
of these moderate gusts to around 30-40 mph down to the lake surface 
today. Southeasterly winds should also downslope across the northern 
and western slopes of the northern Greens and Northeast Kingdom 
today, producing gusts 30-40 mph in parts of Franklin, Orleans, 
Lamoille, Chittenden, Washington, and Orange counties of Vermont. 
Finally, a stronger push Wednesday will shunt the stationary 
boundary southward with northerly breezes developing behind a 
reinforcing boundary. Gusts 20 to 35 mph will be possible Wednesday 
night, with stronger ridge level winds expected. This will make for 
a chilly night as apparent temperatures fall into the mid 20s and 
30s. Conditions likely won't improve much Thursday either, with 
temperatures only reaching the 50s.

KEY MESSAGE 3: A very dynamic pattern is expected to bring changeable 
weather to the region for late week and over the weekend. An upper 
trough will dig into the Great Lakes early Friday, deepening as it 
swings eastward and eventually forming a closed low somewhere 
between Hudson Bay and the Gaspe Peninsula on Saturday. Meanwhile, 
a weak northern stream low over the northern Great Lakes will phase 
with another low located in the Midwest, allowing for an 
intensifying surface low lifting up somewhere in the vicinity of the 
St Lawrence Valley on Friday and eventually into the Canadian 
Maritimes on Saturday. Widespread rain will spread over our region 
on Friday on strong isentropic lift and the nose of a 55+ kt 850 mb 
jet. At the least this jet will make for windy conditions across the 
higher summits, but even lower elevations could be breezy even if 
mixing won't be optimal under steady rainfall. However, a strong 
cold front will quickly cross the region later Friday into Friday 
night, and the influx of colder air and associated steepening lapse 
rates will amplify mixing stronger winds down to the surface. South 
winds of 15 to 25 mph with gusts to 30 mph are likely on Friday, 
potentially stronger in the Champlain Valley and over the higher 
summits. These winds will turn to the west/northwest after the 
frontal passage Friday night and Saturday; note the mean gusts off 
of the long-range ensembles are 35-40 mph, with a 30-50% chance of 
exceeding 40 mph over the Adirondacks, along/east of the spine of 
the Greens, and over Lake Champlain. While we don't anticipate 
needing a Wind Advisory (for gusts greater than 46 mph), trends will 
need to be watched closely going forward. 

The other impact with this system and its strong cold front will be 
rapidly falling temperatures, allowing rain to turn to snow. 
Precipitation will linger longest in the higher terrain, especially 
the favored western slopes as we'll see wrap-around upslope 
northwest flow. Even the wider valleys could see a bit of the white 
stuff Friday night/early Saturday as snow levels look to fall below 
500 ft, particularly in the St Lawrence and northern Champlain 
Valleys. Snow showers will persist over the higher terrain through
